action_trace.summary: Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (safety priorities, ODD boundaries), pain points (failure scenarios, communication gaps), and acceptance criteria (MRM decision logic, validation expectations) grounded in the Apollo Pilot Safety Report's multi-layer safety architecture and MRM requirements.

Generated 9 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals, pain points, and acceptance criteria for AD safety requirements. Questions target failure scenarios, stakeholder perspectives, environmental constraints, prioritization logic, and measurable safety outcomes to ground the multi-layer safety architecture and Minimal Risk Maneuver requirements in user context.

Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (multi-layer safety architecture), pain points (MRM decision logic, failure mode prioritization), and acceptance criteria (safe state transition, ODD compliance, fail-safe validation). Questions decompose the Apollo safety report requirements into actionable dialogue prompts that surface stakeholder assumptions about collision protection, active/functional safety layer interdependencies, and risk maneuver triggers.

End-user (logistics fleet operator) requires autonomous vehicles with multi-layer safety architecture that implements passive, active, and functional safety mechanisms. Critical pain point: systems must execute graceful Minimal Risk Maneuvers (safe zone transitions) rather than abrupt lane stops when critical failures occur, preventing secondary collisions. Expectations center on sensor redundancy, ODD boundary handling, and systematic degradation across highway and urban delivery scenarios.

End-user confirms multi-layer safety architecture requirement with emphasis on Minimal Risk Maneuver execution (safe repositioning vs. in-lane emergency stop) during critical failures. Long-haul logistics context demands fatigue mitigation, fail-safe ODD transitions, and redundant safety mechanisms across highway and urban delivery domains.

End-user requires multi-layer safety architecture with Minimal Risk Maneuver capability to address driver fatigue liability and 2-3 second failure response gaps in long-haul logistics. System must detect critical failures (sensor/localization loss, ODD exit) and execute graceful degradation to safe zones within 1-2 seconds across all operational domains, preventing emergency stops in traffic.

Six clarification questions raised regarding MRM triggering criteria, unsafe stopping conditions, conflicting safety priorities, fail-safe architecture layering, ODD boundary detection, and system response time targets to resolve ambiguities in the multi-layer safety architecture and MRM execution requirements.

Five clarification questions raised to resolve ambiguities in Minimal Risk Maneuver triggering conditions, safety zone definitions, multi-layer safety precedence, system response time targets, and ODD-dependent MRM strategy adaptation. These questions address the gap between high-level safety expectations and concrete operational parameters needed for requirements specification.

Six clarification questions raised to resolve ambiguities in Multi-Layer Safety Architecture and Minimal Risk Maneuver requirements: objective 'unsafe' thresholds, safety layer priority rules, 'safe zone' definitions across road types, system response time targets, ODD transition protocols, and sensor recovery criteria. These clarifications are critical to prevent conflicting safety behaviors and ensure consistent MRM execution across logistics delivery scenarios.

End-user confirms multi-layer safety architecture and MRM concept; requires refinement on: (1) MRM response time windows (<500ms detection, <5s positioning), (2) unsafe in-lane stopping criteria (speed/density/grade thresholds), (3) safety layer conflict resolution (Functional Safety precedence), (4) safe zone definition by road type, (5) sensor fusion latency targets (<200-500ms), and (6) rollover vs. in-lane stopping decision logic. All refinements are grounded in logistics pain points (fatigue, 2-3s response delays, liability exposure).

End-user confirms multi-layer safety architecture necessity based on fatigue and 2-3s response delay pain points. Refinements required: (1) MRM transition timing (detect <500ms, position <5s), (2) unsafe in-lane stopping criteria by road type, (3) safety layer decision hierarchy under conflict, (4) ODD boundary behavior during MRM, (5) sensor loss combination thresholds, (6) safe zone classification logic across road types. Chain-of-Thought: user pain points validate redundancy; user clarification questions expose gaps in failure mode specificity and decision logic that must be resolved before system requirements can be formalized.

End-user validation confirms multi-layer safety architecture is mandatory for fleet operations. MRM requirements refined into dual time windows (sub-second detection-to-decision, 3-5 second execution), road-type-specific unsafe stopping criteria, safe zone definitions, and explicit safety layer precedence hierarchy. System response time target <500ms from failure detection to MRM initiation addresses end-user pain point of driver response delays causing collisions.

Consolidated 8 structured interview records from end-user safety dialogue following ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 elicitation standards. Records formalize multi-layer safety architecture mandate, MRM trigger conditions, response time windows (sub-second detection, 3-5s positioning), context-dependent unsafe stopping criteria, safe zone definitions, safety layer decision precedence, ODD coverage requirements, and fatigue mitigation rationale. All records trace to end-user pain points (2-3s response delay, fleet incidents) and clarification questions. Status: 2 CONFIRMED, 6 REFINED—ready for deployer validation and system requirement derivation.

Synthesized 8 hierarchical user requirements (6 MUST, 2 SHOULD) for autonomous delivery fleet safety. Requirements address multi-layer safety architecture, MRM trigger detection and response timing (<1s initiation, 3-5s positioning), context-specific unsafe stopping criteria across road types, safe zone validation, and safety layer decision precedence. All requirements traced to interview records, end-user pain points (2-3s driver delay), clarification questions, and confirmations. Chain-of-Thought reasoning: (1) Identified core safety concern (driver response delay gap), (2) Decomposed into detection, response, and decision logic layers, (3) Applied context-specificity (road type thresholds), (4) Resolved conflicts via precedence hierarchy, (5) Prioritized via MoSCoW based on criticality and confirmation status.

Targeted interviewer questions for Deployer probe: (1) computational latency budgets for sub-second MRM initiation; (2) sensor redundancy architecture and failure detection timing; (3) localization validation and ODD boundary detection mechanisms; (4) safe-zone database accessibility and real-time lookup performance; (5) brake system redundancy and graceful degradation; (6) safety-layer precedence arbitration logic; (7) rollover-risk assessment and shoulder-geometry validation; (8) traffic-density monitoring for dynamic unsafe-criteria evaluation; (9) functional safety certification levels (ISO 26262 ASIL) and SIL targets; (10) MRM scalability across diverse ODD scenarios and edge cases where no safe zone exists. Questions apply 5W1H and Socratic techniques to decompose infrastructure constraints, security mandates, and scalability expectations against multi-layer safety architecture and MRM response-time requirements.

Eight targeted deployer questions probe infrastructure constraints (compute latency, sensor architecture), safety layer arbitration logic, real-time safe zone validation, rollover risk measurement, ODD scalability, security isolation, and fleet-wide consistency. Questions directly address sub-second MRM initiation, 3-5 second shoulder positioning, and precedence hierarchy implementation to validate feasibility of multi-layer safety architecture requirements.

Chain-of-Thought Analysis: The Deployer must address three critical dimensions: (1) Infrastructure—real-time latency budgets, sensor redundancy, and V2I availability to support sub-second MRM initiation and dynamic safe-zone validation; (2) Security—cybersecurity controls for MRM trigger integrity, safe-zone database authenticity, and audit logging for regulatory traceability; (3) Scalability—fleet-wide safe-zone database architecture, vehicle-class parameter variance, and phased rollout strategy. Key unresolved tension: MRM precedence hierarchy conflicts (Passive vs. Active Safety) when embankment rollover risk contradicts highway in-lane stopping risk—clarification needed on final decision authority and fallback strategies for unmapped terrain.

Deployer response establishes infrastructure constraints (edge compute <100ms, N+1 sensor redundancy, immutable MRM logic), security mandates (code signing, V2I authentication, offline safe zone fallback), scalability targets (10,000+ geofenced zones, 50+ sensor streams), and operational procedures (MRM sequence <1s initiation, unsafe in-lane criteria by road type, safety layer precedence with rollover protection). Cost-performance trade-offs justify dual-channel sensors and offline safe zone database for autonomous delivery fleet operations across 5 road types.

Chain-of-Thought analysis reveals infrastructure constraints require operational context refinement before implementation feasibility can be assessed.

Deployer raises 5 critical clarifications on latency budget decomposition, sensor redundancy architecture conflicts, safety layer precedence execution under time constraints, code immutability vs. runtime MRM adaptation, and fail-safe fallback specification. These questions target infrastructure constraints (IC-001 through IC-005), security mandates (SM-001), and operational feasibility gaps between static pre-loaded databases and dynamic real-time safe zone validation within sub-second MRM initiation windows.

Comprehensive operating environment specification for AD autonomous delivery fleet captures: PREEMPT_RT edge compute platform with <100ms latency budget, redundant dual-channel sensor fusion (LiDAR+camera+radar+GPS/IMU), hardwired fail-safe deceleration fallback, pre-loaded road geometry database with real-time traffic validation, immutable safety-critical code via hardware security module, and deterministic MRM execution within <1 second failure detection to initiation with 3-5 second shoulder positioning window. Deployment architecture resolves latency decomposition conflicts, hybrid database strategy, and sensor redundancy constraints while maintaining ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 traceability and multi-layer safety precedence hierarchy.
